Patriclan — the main unit of Ovaherero patrilineal descent and the basis of the Oupweye religion.
Plural: otuzo. Surnames and homesteads belonging to the same patrilineage are grouped under one oruzo.

The book is structured around the Ovaherero patrilineal descent systems called otuzo, and the patriclan oruzo which is the basis of the Ovaherero religion Oupweye./Embo indi ra tjangwa ongondoroka notuzo twOvaherero, tjinga oruzo e ri ongunḓe onene yongamburiro yOvaherero indji yOupweye.
Surnames and homesteads belonging to a patriclan (oruzo).
Singular: onganda.

The surnames and homesteads that belong to the same patrilineage are grouped together under each patriclan to help the reader to easily trace the homesteads that belong to one patriclan./Ozonganda nḓe na oruzo rumwe za tjangwa kehi yoruzo rumwe kokutja pe yandja oupupu komurese okutjiwa ozonganda ozonḓamumwe poo nḓa za momuze umwe.
Sub-clans or branches within a patriclan (oruzo).
The emblem of a patriclan — an animal or natural feature that identifies the oruzo.
Taboos and prohibitions observed by members of a patriclan (oruzo).
The relatedness between patriclans — clans that recognise a common bond and do not intermarry.
Praise names — the praise poetry of a homestead or patriclan, recited to honour the clan and its cattle.

The book further narrates the distinct features of each patriclan in terms of totems, taboos, patriclans that collaborate and praise poems of surnames and homesteads./Komurungu embo mari raisa oviuṋe vyoruzo aruhe tjimuna ondwezu yoruzo ndwo, ovizerika, otuzo tu tu huhurasana nomitango poo omiṱanḓu vyozonganda zoruzo ndo.
Homestead; also the surname associated with it. Plural: ozonganda.
Plural of oruzo: the patriclans of the Ovaherero.
The Herero people — a Bantu-speaking people of Namibia, Botswana and Angola.
Praise goes to GOD who spared the Ovaherero from the genocide./Ondangu nohivirikiro me yandja ku NDJAMBI ngwa yama Ovaherero kotjiṱiro otjindjandja.
In 1884, South West Africa (currently known as Namibia) became a German territory./Mombura ndji 1884, Osuid-Wes Afrika (nai nda rira Onamibia) otji ra rira okarukondwa kehi rOvandoitji.

All the patriclans and praise poems in this book were collected from the Ovaherero community living in Namibia./Otuzo atuhe nomitango avihe mbi ri membo ndi vya wongwa okuza motjiwaṋa tjOvaherero mbe hupira mo Namibia.

I use the term Ovaherero to include the various tribes forming the Ovaherero group and speaking a common language, which are the Ovahimba, Ovaherero, Ovatjimba and Ovambanderu./Ami mba ungurisa embo “Ovaherero” okuhitisa omihoko avihe mbi wira kehi yOuherero nu mbi hungira eraka rimwe mbi ri Ovahimba, Ovaherero, Ovatjimba nOvambanderu.

This book about the patriclans (called otuzo) tackles an aspect of Otjiherero and folklore which previously has not been in written form, although all praise poems of homesteads are known./Embo rOtuzo twOvaherero mari tara keraka rOtjiherero noviuṋe vyaro ovinanḓengu mbi hi ya tjangwa, nandarire kutja oviuṋe ohunga notuzo nomitango vyozonganda vi tjiukwa.

The book attempts to preserve and document this intangible heritage, which is in the form of oral traditions and expressions, before it disappears./Embo mari pwike oviuṋe ovinanḓengu imbi ovihaṋuṋungwa mbi hungirwa kotjinyo momatjangwa ngunda avi hi ya zenga.
